author: reek
body: A Codex program can write a file. This is the test that says so, and it says it by writing one and then reading it back through a path that shares no code with the writer: fat16-read-text walks the directory, follows the cluster chain and decodes the bytes, exactly as it did before any of this existed.

author: reek
body: The bytes matter as much as the round trip. Codex Text is CCE internally, and a FAT16 short name and a file's contents are ASCII. A writer that put CCE on the disk would round-trip perfectly here -- our reader would decode what our writer encoded, and the two would agree forever -- while producing a file no other reader on earth could open. That is not a hypothetical: it is what shipped a TLS hostname and every key-schedule label in CCE. So the harness checks the raw bytes host-side as well, and this test pins the half it can: the size the directory entry records, which is a byte count and not a character count, and would be wrong the moment the encoding was.
